items.label: section_header
items.text: KEY POINT

items.label: text
items.text: Iron needs oxygen and water to rust. The rusting of iron is discussed in Chapter 14.

items.label: text
items.text: Safety Note: Iron filings can irritate the skin and are a particular hazard if they get in the eyes.

items.label: section_header
items.text: ACTIVITY 2

items.label: section_header
items.text: PRACTICAL: USING THE RUSTING OF IRON

items.label: text
items.text: Iron rusts in damp air, using up oxygen as it does so. We can use this reaction to determine how much oxygen there is in the air.

items.label: list_item
items.text: Figure 13.3 This apparatus can be used to find the percentage of oxygen in the air.

items.label: text
items.text: We will use the apparatus from Figure 13.3, but before we start we need to know the volume of air present in the apparatus. We can find this by filling up the conical flask and connecting tube with water and then transferring the water to a measuring cylinder. On the conical flask we mark the position of the bung and only fill with water to that point. We will assume that the small volume occupied by the iron filings is negligible (very small compared to the overall volume).

items.label: text
items.text: The procedure for the experiment is as follows:

items.label: list_item
items.text: Set up the apparatus as shown in Figure 13.3.

items.label: list_item
items.text: Put wet iron filings into the conical flask.

items.label: list_item
items.text: Record the initial reading on the gas syringe.

items.label: list_item
items.text: Leave the apparatus in place for about a week, until the reading on the gas syringe stops changing.

items.label: list_item
items.text: Record the final reading on the gas syringe.

items.label: table
items.text:
| volume of air in conical flask/cm³   |   130 |
|--------------------------------------|-------|
| volume of air in connecting tube/cm³ |    12 |
| initial reading on gas syringe/cm³   |    92 |
| final reading on gas syringe/cm3     |    43 |

items.label: text
items.text: So, the total volume of air inside the apparatus at the beginning of the experiment is 130 + 12 + 92 = 234 cm³.

items.label: text
items.text: The total volume of 'air' in the apparatus at the end = 130 + 12 + 43 =185cm³

items.label: text
items.text: Volume of oxygen used up = 234 - 185 = 49 cm³

items.label: text
items.text: The percentage of oxygen in the air is 49/234 × 100 = 21%.

items.label: text
items.text: Sometimes when you do this experiment, the answer comes out as less than 21%. Possible reasons for this could be:

items.label: list_item
items.text: The experiment was not left set up for long enough. The iron has not had enough chance to react with all the oxygen in the apparatus.

items.label: list_item
items.text: Not enough iron was added at the beginning. The iron must be in excess, that is, there must be enough iron to react with all the oxygen present.
